meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering B4.1 Adaptation to environment, guide topic B4.1.
final_note: You worked through B4.1 Adaptation to environment — 8 guide statements.

concepts.def: The place in which a community, species, population or organism lives. A description of a habitat can include its geographical location (for example the Atlantic coasts of western Europe), its physical location (for example the seaward slopes of foredunes) and the type of ecosystem (for example a coastal sand dune system).
A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time. A population lives in a habitat; it is not itself the habitat.

All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area. A community lives in a habitat; the habitat is the place, and the community is the living part of the ecosystem that occupies it.

The non-living physical and chemical conditions of a habitat, such as temperature, water availability, light intensity, salinity, soil or water pH, oxygen availability and wind. Organisms have adaptations, evolved by natural selection, that allow them to survive and reproduce within the abiotic conditions of their habitat.

A grass species adapted to the abiotic environment of coastal sand dunes, where sand drains freely, wind and salt spray are strong, nutrients are scarce and sand is repeatedly deposited over the plant. Its leaves roll inwards in dry conditions, with the stomata in grooves on the inner surface and hairs that trap humid air, reducing transpiration; the outer surface has a thick waxy cuticle; extensive rhizomes and deep roots anchor the plant and stabilize the sand; and vertical growth is stimulated by burial, so the plant grows up through newly deposited sand.

Tree species adapted to mangrove swamps: tidal, saline, waterlogged mud that is low in oxygen. The grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) has pneumatophores for gas exchange and salt glands on its leaves that secrete excess salt; the red mangrove (Rhizophora) has stilt (prop) roots for support in soft mud and excludes most salt at its roots by ultrafiltration. Both maintain a low water potential in their cells so that water can be absorbed from seawater, and both produce propagules that germinate while still attached to the parent tree.

A vertical root that grows upward from the horizontal roots of a mangrove such as Avicennia marina and projects above the mud into the air. Pneumatophores carry pores (lenticels) through which oxygen diffuses into the root system, allowing aerobic respiration in roots buried in waterlogged, anaerobic mud.

A non-living factor of the environment that can vary from place to place or over time and affect where a species can live. Examples for plants include temperature, water availability, light intensity, soil pH, salinity and the availability of mineral nutrients; examples for animals include temperature, water availability, salinity, pH and, in aquatic habitats, the concentration of dissolved oxygen.

The range of values of an abiotic variable within which a species can survive, given by its adaptations. Within the range there is an optimum zone in which individuals grow and reproduce best, flanked by zones of stress in which they survive but with reduced growth or reproduction; beyond the limits of tolerance the species cannot survive, so it is absent from places where the variable lies outside its range.

The pattern of where a species is found. Distribution is affected by abiotic variables because each species has a range of tolerance for each variable: a species is restricted to places where every abiotic variable lies within its range of tolerance.

An abiotic variable that restricts the distribution, growth or abundance of a species because its value lies at or beyond the edge of the species' range of tolerance. Along a gradient of an abiotic variable, the point at which a species disappears indicates a limit of its tolerance for that factor.

A line laid across a habitat along which the distribution of species is recorded, usually by placing quadrats at regular intervals and recording the abundance (for example percentage cover or counts) of each species in each quadrat. Abiotic variables such as temperature, light intensity and soil pH are measured at the same points, often with sensors, so that changes in the distribution of a species can be correlated with changes in an abiotic variable.

A habitat that has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species, such as a hay meadow, a grazed heath or a coppiced woodland. Transect data for correlating species distribution with an abiotic variable should be collected from a natural or semi-natural habitat.

concepts.term: Correlation between distribution and an abiotic variable
concepts.def: A relationship in which the abundance of a species changes as an abiotic variable changes along a transect. A correlation is consistent with the variable limiting the species but does not prove that it does so: other variables that change along the same transect, or biotic factors, could be responsible, so an experiment is needed to establish cause.

A marine ecosystem built up from the calcium carbonate skeletons deposited by reef-building corals. Corals are colonial animals (cnidarians) whose polyps secrete calcium carbonate and contain zooxanthellae, so reef formation requires the physical conditions in which both the polyps and the zooxanthellae can function.

Photosynthetic unicellular algae (dinoflagellates) that live inside the tissues of reef-building coral polyps in a mutualistic relationship. They supply the coral with carbon compounds from photosynthesis, which is why reef-building corals require shallow, clear water that light can penetrate.

Reef-building corals require: shallow water, generally less than about 50 m deep, so that light reaches the zooxanthellae; clear water, because suspended sediment reduces light and smothers polyps; warm water, typically between about 23 °C and 29 °C; salinity close to that of the open ocean, roughly 32 to 42 parts per thousand, so reefs do not form where rivers dilute seawater; and a pH of about 8.0 to 8.4, since a fall in pH lowers the carbonate ion concentration needed for calcification.

A graph with mean annual temperature on one axis and mean annual precipitation on the other, on which the distribution of terrestrial biomes is plotted as regions. For any given combination of temperature and rainfall pattern, one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop; the graph therefore shows that these two abiotic factors are the main determinants of terrestrial biome distribution.

A group of ecosystems, which may be on different continents, that have similar communities because they experience similar abiotic conditions and because convergent evolution has produced organisms with similar adaptations. The species are not the same in each ecosystem of a biome; it is the community structure and the types of adaptation that are similar.

The independent evolution of similar features in lineages that are not closely related, because natural selection in similar environments favours similar adaptations. The water-storing stems and spines of cacti in the Americas and of euphorbias in Africa are an example: they arose separately in different plant families in response to similar hot desert conditions.

concepts.term: Climate conditions of the major biomes
concepts.def: Tropical forest: hot all year (mean annual temperature typically 20 to 30 °C) with very high rainfall, generally above 2000 mm a year, and little seasonal variation. Temperate forest: moderate temperatures with warm summers and cool winters, and rainfall of roughly 750 to 1500 mm a year spread through the year. Taiga (boreal forest): long, cold winters and short, mild summers, with low to moderate precipitation, much of it as snow. Grassland: rainfall too low or too seasonal to support forest, roughly 250 to 750 mm a year in temperate grassland, with a wide range of temperatures. Tundra: very cold, with mean annual temperatures below freezing, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation generally below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil (permafrost). Hot desert: precipitation below about 250 mm a year, very high daytime temperatures and a large difference between day and night temperatures.

concepts.term: Hot desert adaptations: saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea)
concepts.def: A plant of the Sonoran Desert adapted to extreme heat and scarce, unpredictable rainfall. Spines replace leaves, reducing the surface area for transpiration and deterring herbivores; the green stem photosynthesizes and is covered by a thick waxy cuticle; the stem is pleated, so it can swell to store water after rain; stomata open at night rather than during the hot day; and the roots are shallow but spread widely, absorbing rain from a large area before it drains away or evaporates.

concepts.term: Hot desert adaptations: fennec fox (Vulpes zerda)
concepts.def: A small mammal of the Sahara. Its very large ears, with many blood vessels close to the surface, radiate heat and cool the fox without loss of water, and also give acute hearing for locating prey; it is nocturnal, sheltering in a burrow during the heat of the day; its pale coat reflects sunlight; thick fur on the soles of the feet protects them from hot sand; and its kidneys produce concentrated urine, so it can obtain most of its water from food and rarely needs to drink.

concepts.term: Tropical rainforest adaptations: kapok tree (Ceiba pentandra)
concepts.def: An emergent tree that grows to over 60 m in tropical rainforest, where rainfall exceeds 2000 mm a year and most nutrients are held in living biomass rather than in the shallow, leached soil. Its buttress roots spread out above the ground and support the very tall trunk in shallow soil, while a wide, shallow network of roots absorbs nutrients from the thin layer of decomposing litter. It grows rapidly to reach full sunlight above the canopy and its smooth bark discourages climbing plants.

concepts.term: Tropical rainforest adaptations: black-handed spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi)
concepts.def: A mammal of the canopy of Central American rainforest that feeds mainly on ripe fruit. Its prehensile tail, with a hairless friction pad near the tip, acts as a fifth limb and can support the whole body, freeing the hands to reach fruit at the ends of branches; its long limbs and hook-like hands with reduced thumbs allow it to swing beneath branches (brachiation) as it moves through the canopy; and it is active by day, when it can see ripe fruit.

mcqs.q: Which statement gives the meaning of the term habitat as it is used in ecology?
options: The place in which a community, species, population or single organism lives.
The role that a species plays in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on.
A large region of the Earth that shares one type of climate, such as tundra.
The set of organisms of different species that live together in one area.
mcqs.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
mcqs.explain: This is the definition used in the guide. A habitat is a place, and it can be the place where a whole community lives or where one organism lives; it is described by geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.
rationales: This is the definition used in the guide. A habitat is a place, and it can be the place where a whole community lives or where one organism lives; it is described by geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.
A student who merges an organism's way of life with where it lives picks this. The role a species plays is a different idea from its habitat, which is the place in which it lives.

A student who has met 'the tundra habitat' in general reading picks this. A region of shared climate is a biome; a habitat is the place where a particular organism, population or community lives and can be very small.

A student who attaches the word to the organisms rather than the place picks this. The organisms of different species living together are the community; the habitat is the place in which that community lives.

mcqs.q: Marram grass (Ammophila arenaria) grows on the seaward slopes of sand dunes along the Atlantic coasts of western Europe. Which of the following is a description of the habitat of marram grass?
options: All of the marram grass plants that grow on one particular dune system on the coast of Wales.
The seaward slopes of foredunes in the coastal sand dune ecosystems of western Europe.
The marram grass, sea holly, sand lizards and dune beetles living together on a dune.
The temperate grassland biome, in which rainfall is too low for forest to develop.
mcqs.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
mcqs.explain: A habitat description gives the geographical location (western Europe), the physical location (seaward slopes of foredunes) and the type of ecosystem (coastal sand dune). This option gives all three.
rationales: A student who confuses the population with the place picks this. All the marram plants on one dune system are a population of marram grass; the habitat is the place in which that population lives.
A habitat description gives the geographical location (western Europe), the physical location (seaward slopes of foredunes) and the type of ecosystem (coastal sand dune). This option gives all three.
A student who treats the habitat as the organisms found there picks this. The species living together on the foredune make up the community; the habitat is the foredune itself.

A student who equates habitat with biome picks this because marram is a grass. A biome is a group of ecosystems with similar climate; sand dunes are a coastal ecosystem shaped by sand and salt spray, not temperate grassland, and a habitat is a place, not a biome.

mcqs.q: In dry, windy weather the leaves of marram grass roll inwards, so that the stomata, which lie in grooves on the inner surface, open into an enclosed space lined with hairs. How does this help marram grass to survive on a sand dune, where water drains away quickly?
options: Sea spray and dew collect inside the rolled leaf and are absorbed through the stomata, supplying the plant with water.
The hairs increase the surface area from which water evaporates, so that the leaf is cooled more effectively in the sun.
Humid air is trapped around the stomata, lowering the water vapour concentration gradient and slowing transpiration.
The stomata inside the roll are held permanently closed, so the plant loses no water while the leaf is rolled.
mcqs.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
mcqs.explain: Water vapour diffuses out of stomata down a concentration gradient. Inside the rolled leaf the hairs hold a layer of still, humid air, so the gradient between the leaf interior and the air outside the stomata is small and the rate of transpiration is reduced. This conserves water in a habitat where sand holds little.
rationales: A student who thinks leaves take in water through their stomata picks this. Marram grass absorbs water through its deep roots and rhizomes; stomata are pores for gas exchange, and the rolled leaf is an adaptation for reducing the water lost through them.

A student who believes transpiration exists to cool the plant picks this. On a dune, water is the scarce resource, so the adaptation works by reducing evaporation, not increasing it; the hairs trap humid air rather than providing an evaporating surface.

Water vapour diffuses out of stomata down a concentration gradient. Inside the rolled leaf the hairs hold a layer of still, humid air, so the gradient between the leaf interior and the air outside the stomata is small and the rate of transpiration is reduced. This conserves water in a habitat where sand holds little.

A student who thinks dry-habitat plants shut their stomata for good picks this. Stomata must open to admit carbon dioxide for photosynthesis; the rolled leaf reduces the water lost while they are open rather than abolishing it.

mcqs.q: The grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) grows in tidal mud that is waterlogged and almost free of oxygen. From its horizontal roots it sends up pneumatophores, which project vertically out of the mud into the air. What is the function of the pneumatophores?
options: They absorb water vapour from the humid air above the mud to supplement the uptake by the roots.
They anchor the tree against the tidal currents by spreading its weight across the soft mud.
They secrete excess salt taken up from seawater onto their surfaces, where the tide washes it away.
They let oxygen diffuse from the air into the root tissues buried in anaerobic mud.
mcqs.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
mcqs.explain: Roots need oxygen for aerobic respiration, and waterlogged mud contains almost none. Pneumatophores carry lenticels above the mud surface through which oxygen enters and diffuses down to the buried root system.
rationales: A student who thinks plants absorb water through above-ground surfaces picks this. Water is taken up in liquid form by the roots; the problem the pneumatophores solve is the lack of oxygen in the mud, not a lack of water.

A student who has seen the arching stilt roots of Rhizophora and assumes all aerial roots give support picks this. Avicennia's pneumatophores are thin, pencil-like roots that give little support; their function is gas exchange.
A student who reasons that salt must leave by the route it entered picks this. Avicennia secretes excess salt from salt glands on its leaves, not from its roots; pneumatophores are for gas exchange.

Roots need oxygen for aerobic respiration, and waterlogged mud contains almost none. Pneumatophores carry lenticels above the mud surface through which oxygen enters and diffuses down to the buried root system.

mcqs.q: Mangrove trees grow with their roots in seawater, which has a much lower water potential than the soil water available to most land plants. Which statement describes an adaptation of mangroves to the high salinity of their habitat?
options: Salt glands on the leaves of Avicennia secrete excess salt, and the roots of Rhizophora exclude most salt by ultrafiltration.
The roots take up seawater freely because mangroves require large amounts of sodium chloride for their metabolism.
Pneumatophores pump salt out of the roots and back into the mud, keeping the sap of the tree free of salt.
The leaves absorb rainwater directly, so the tree does not need to take up any water through its roots from the sea.
mcqs.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
mcqs.explain: These are the two main strategies of mangrove trees: preventing most salt from entering at the roots (Rhizophora) and removing salt that does enter by secreting it from glands on the leaf surface (Avicennia). Together with a low water potential in their cells, this allows water uptake from seawater.
rationales: These are the two main strategies of mangrove trees: preventing most salt from entering at the roots (Rhizophora) and removing salt that does enter by secreting it from glands on the leaf surface (Avicennia). Together with a low water potential in their cells, this allows water uptake from seawater.

A student who assumes that a plant found only in salty places must need salt picks this. Mangroves tolerate salt rather than requiring it; their adaptations limit and remove salt because it is a stress, not a nutrient they need in quantity.

A student who thinks excess salt leaves through the roots picks this. Pneumatophores are aerial roots for gas exchange; salt is excluded at the root surface or secreted from the leaves, and the sap of mangroves does contain salt.

A student who thinks leaves absorb water picks this. Mangroves take up water through their roots from seawater, which is possible because their cells maintain a water potential lower than that of the sea.

mcqs.q: A study reports that brown trout survive in water between about 0 °C and 25 °C and grow fastest between 10 °C and 16 °C. During a hot summer the water temperature in a river rises from 14 °C to 22 °C. Which statement correctly applies the idea of a range of tolerance?
options: 22 °C is outside the trout's range of tolerance, so the population in the river will die out before the end of summer.
22 °C is inside the trout's range of tolerance but outside its optimum, so the fish survive but are under stress.
The trout will adapt during their lifetime, widening their range of tolerance to include the new temperature.
Temperature cannot limit where trout live, because unlike plants they can swim away from unfavourable water.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
mcqs.explain: The range of tolerance (0 to 25 °C) is wider than the optimum range (10 to 16 °C). At 22 °C the trout are in a zone of stress: they survive, but growth and reproduction are reduced. Only above 25 °C would the limit of tolerance be exceeded.
rationales: A student who takes the optimum range to be the whole range of tolerance picks this. The upper limit of tolerance given is 25 °C; 22 °C lies in the zone of stress, where trout survive with reduced growth.

The range of tolerance (0 to 25 °C) is wider than the optimum range (10 to 16 °C). At 22 °C the trout are in a zone of stress: they survive, but growth and reproduction are reduced. Only above 25 °C would the limit of tolerance be exceeded.
A student who uses 'adapt' in its everyday sense picks this. A range of tolerance is set by inherited adaptations; individuals cannot extend it, and in any case 22 °C is already within the range.

A student who thinks abiotic variables affect only plants picks this. Swimming away from warm water is precisely how temperature limits the distribution of trout: they are absent from water outside their range of tolerance.

mcqs.q: Which statement about abiotic variables and the distribution of species is correct?
options: Only the distribution of plants is limited by abiotic variables, because animals are able to move away from unfavourable conditions.
A species with a wide range of tolerance for temperature is found everywhere that the temperature lies within that range.
Adaptations give a species a range of tolerance for each abiotic variable, and it is absent where a variable is outside that range.
An abiotic variable is any feature of the environment, whether it is living or non-living, that differs between one place and another.
mcqs.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
mcqs.explain: This is the relationship the guide sets out: adaptations determine the range of tolerance, and distribution is limited to places where every abiotic variable lies within the species' range.
rationales: A student who thinks of animals as escaping rather than being limited picks this. Animals have ranges of tolerance for temperature, salinity, pH and dissolved oxygen, and moving away from unsuitable conditions is how those limits shape distribution.

A student who considers one abiotic variable at a time picks this. Every abiotic variable must be within the range of tolerance; a place with a suitable temperature may still be too dry, too dark or too saline for the species.
This is the relationship the guide sets out: adaptations determine the range of tolerance, and distribution is limited to places where every abiotic variable lies within the species' range.

A student who has lost the meaning of the prefix 'a-' picks this. Abiotic variables are non-living factors such as temperature, water, light, pH and salinity; predators, competitors and food are biotic factors.

mcqs.q: A student lays a 30 m transect from the seaward edge of a salt marsh up the shore, placing a quadrat every 5 m. In each quadrat they record the percentage cover of sea lavender and measure the salinity of the soil water in parts per thousand (ppt) with a conductivity sensor. The results are: 0 m, salinity 35 ppt, cover 0%; 5 m, 32, 10%; 10 m, 28, 35%; 15 m, 24, 60%; 20 m, 20, 55%; 25 m, 16, 20%; 30 m, 12, 0%. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Salinity has no effect on sea lavender, because cover is zero at both the highest and the lowest salinity recorded.
The transect proves that salinity is the cause of the distribution, because cover changes wherever salinity changes.
Individual sea lavender plants adjust their salt tolerance to match the salinity of the quadrat in which they are growing.
Cover peaks at intermediate salinity, consistent with a range of tolerance whose optimum lies near 20 to 24 ppt.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
mcqs.explain: Cover is zero at 35 ppt and at 12 ppt, rises to a maximum of 60% at 24 and 55% at 20, and falls on either side. This hump-shaped pattern is what a range of tolerance predicts: limits at the extremes and an optimum between them. The data show a correlation; they do not by themselves prove causation.
rationales: A student who expects a correlation to be a straight-line trend picks this. Absence at both extremes with a peak between them is exactly the pattern a limiting abiotic variable produces, so it is evidence for an effect, not against one.

A student who treats a matching pattern as proof picks this. Up a salt marsh, salinity, time submerged, soil moisture and competition all change together, so the transect shows a correlation but cannot prove which variable is the cause.

A student who thinks individuals adapt to wherever they find themselves picks this. The tolerance range is an inherited property of the species; the data show where the species can and cannot survive, not plants changing their tolerance.

Cover is zero at 35 ppt and at 12 ppt, rises to a maximum of 60% at 24 and 55% at 20, and falls on either side. This hump-shaped pattern is what a range of tolerance predicts: limits at the extremes and an optimum between them. The data show a correlation; they do not by themselves prove causation.

mcqs.q: Students are required to collect transect data from a natural or semi-natural habitat. Which of these sites is semi-natural?
options: A hay meadow that is cut once each year but is dominated by wild grasses and wildflowers.
A field of wheat grown from sown seed, with wild poppies growing along its margins.
A garden lawn sown with a bought seed mixture and mown every week through the summer.
A peat bog in a remote upland with no history of drainage, grazing or other management.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
mcqs.explain: A semi-natural habitat has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Annual cutting is human influence; the wild grasses and flowers that dominate make the meadow semi-natural.
rationales: A semi-natural habitat has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Annual cutting is human influence; the wild grasses and flowers that dominate make the meadow semi-natural.
A student who takes the presence of any wild species as the test picks this. The field is dominated by a cultivated crop; a few wild poppies at the edge do not make it semi-natural.
A student who counts any green outdoor site as semi-natural picks this. A sown lawn is dominated by cultivated grass varieties, so it is not semi-natural.

A student who thinks semi-natural means untouched picks this. A bog with no human influence is a natural habitat, which is also acceptable for fieldwork, but the question asks which site is semi-natural: influenced by humans yet dominated by wild species.

mcqs.q: A student wants to find out whether the distribution of dog's mercury, a woodland plant, is correlated with light intensity across the boundary between a field and a wood. Which procedure is most appropriate?
options: Place quadrats at random coordinates within the wood only, because the field contains no dog's mercury and so gives no useful data.
Place quadrats at regular intervals along a transect from the field into the wood, recording percentage cover and a light-sensor reading at each quadrat.
Record the species present in one large quadrat in the field and one large quadrat in the wood, since two contrasting sites are enough to show a correlation.
Count the plants in quadrats along the transect but take one light reading at the wood edge, because light does not vary within a habitat.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
mcqs.explain: A transect samples the gradient of light from open field to shaded wood at many points, and pairing a cover value with a sensor reading at each quadrat gives the data needed to test for a correlation.
rationales: A student who sees empty quadrats as wasted picks this. Quadrats with zero cover at high light intensity are essential data: they mark the limit of the species' range and provide the contrast without which no correlation can be shown.

A transect samples the gradient of light from open field to shaded wood at many points, and pairing a cover value with a sensor reading at each quadrat gives the data needed to test for a correlation.
A student who carries a two-treatment experimental design into fieldwork picks this. Two sites can show a difference, but a correlation needs many sampling points across the gradient of the variable.

A student who thinks an abiotic variable has one value for a whole habitat picks this. Light intensity falls steeply from the field into the wood, and it must be measured at every quadrat so that each cover value is paired with the light there.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the conditions needed for a coral reef to form is correct?
options: The water must be deep, so that the coral polyps are shielded from the damaging effects of bright sunlight.
The water should be turbid and rich in suspended sediment, which supplies food to the polyps.
The water must be shallow and clear enough for light to reach the zooxanthellae in the coral tissue.
The water should be as warm as possible, because calcification speeds up with every rise in temperature.
mcqs.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
mcqs.explain: Reef-building corals depend on photosynthetic zooxanthellae in their tissues. Depth and clarity are conditions for reef formation because both determine whether enough light reaches the algae; reefs form in clear water generally less than about 50 m deep.
rationales: A student who pictures corals as deep-sea animals picks this. The polyps' zooxanthellae need light for photosynthesis, so reef-building corals are confined to shallow water where light penetrates.

A student who reasons that more particles means more food for polyps picks this. Suspended sediment cuts off light from the zooxanthellae and can smother the polyps; clarity is one of the conditions required.

Reef-building corals depend on photosynthetic zooxanthellae in their tissues. Depth and clarity are conditions for reef formation because both determine whether enough light reaches the algae; reefs form in clear water generally less than about 50 m deep.

A student who extrapolates 'corals need warm water' without an upper limit picks this. Corals have a range of tolerance for temperature, typically about 23 to 29 °C; water that is too warm causes stress and bleaching.

mcqs.q: Reef-building corals deposit skeletons of calcium carbonate. As the oceans absorb more carbon dioxide, the average pH of surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 and the concentration of carbonate ions has decreased. Which statement best explains why this threatens the formation of coral reefs?
options: Seawater at pH 8.1 is acidic, so it dissolves the calcium carbonate of existing coral skeletons directly.
The extra dissolved carbon dioxide is toxic to the coral polyps, which die before they can deposit any skeleton.
A fall of only 0.1 pH units is far too small to affect any organism, so the threat to reefs has been greatly overstated.
Fewer carbonate ions are available, so calcification slows and may not keep pace with reef erosion.
mcqs.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
mcqs.explain: Corals build skeleton by combining calcium ions with carbonate ions. Dissolved carbon dioxide releases hydrogen ions that combine with carbonate ions, lowering their concentration, so deposition of calcium carbonate slows. A reef persists only if deposition outpaces the constant erosion by waves and boring organisms.
rationales: A student who takes the word 'acidification' literally picks this. A pH of 8.1 is still alkaline; the water has become less alkaline, and the harm comes from reduced carbonate ion availability slowing calcification, not from acid dissolving reefs.

A student who treats carbon dioxide as a poison picks this. Carbon dioxide at these concentrations does not poison the polyps; its effect is chemical, reducing the carbonate ion concentration on which calcification depends.
A student who reads the pH scale as linear picks this. pH is logarithmic: a fall of 0.1 units is an increase of about 26% in hydrogen ion concentration, enough to reduce carbonate ions measurably.

Corals build skeleton by combining calcium ions with carbonate ions. Dissolved carbon dioxide releases hydrogen ions that combine with carbonate ions, lowering their concentration, so deposition of calcium carbonate slows. A reef persists only if deposition outpaces the constant erosion by waves and boring organisms.

mcqs.q: A biome distribution graph has mean annual temperature on one axis and mean annual precipitation on the other. Region X has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 150 mm of precipitation a year; region Y has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 3000 mm a year. What does the graph predict?
options: Hot desert is likely to develop in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because rainfall separates them at this temperature.
Tropical forest is likely in both regions, because it is the temperature of 26 °C that determines which biome forms.
Grassland is likely in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because grassland forms wherever it is too dry for trees.
No prediction is possible without knowing the latitude of each region, because latitude rather than climate sets the biome.
mcqs.specStatementText: Temperature and rainfall set the biome
mcqs.explain: For any combination of temperature and rainfall pattern one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop. At 26 °C, precipitation below about 250 mm a year gives hot desert, while precipitation above about 2000 mm a year gives tropical forest.
rationales: For any combination of temperature and rainfall pattern one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop. At 26 °C, precipitation below about 250 mm a year gives hot desert, while precipitation above about 2000 mm a year gives tropical forest.
A student who thinks temperature alone sets the biome picks this. The graph has two axes because both variables matter: 150 mm of rain a year cannot support forest at any temperature.
A student who extends grassland down to zero rainfall picks this. Grassland occupies an intermediate band of precipitation; below about 250 mm a year the graph shows desert.

A student who has memorized biomes as latitude bands picks this. Latitude matters only through its effect on climate; the graph predicts the biome from temperature and precipitation wherever on Earth the region is.

mcqs.q: Cacti of the deserts of the Americas and euphorbias of the deserts of southern Africa both have swollen, water-storing stems and spines, yet they belong to different plant families. Which explanation is correct?
options: The similar appearance shows that cacti and euphorbias share a recent common ancestor that spread to both continents.
Similar abiotic conditions selected for similar adaptations in unrelated lineages, an example of convergent evolution.
Hot desert is one biome, so its community is the same on every continent and each plant in it has the desert form.
Individual plants of any family develop spines and swollen stems when they grow in dry conditions during their lifetime.
mcqs.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities
mcqs.explain: Natural selection in similar hot desert conditions favoured water storage and reduced leaf area in both families independently. Convergent evolution of this kind is one reason the ecosystems of a biome have similar communities even though their species differ.
rationales: A student who equates similarity with close relationship picks this. The question states that they belong to different families; the similarity arose independently and is not inherited from a shared recent ancestor.

Natural selection in similar hot desert conditions favoured water storage and reduced leaf area in both families independently. Convergent evolution of this kind is one reason the ecosystems of a biome have similar communities even though their species differ.

A student who expects a biome to contain the same community of species everywhere picks this. The ecosystems of a biome have similar communities, not identical ones: cacti and euphorbias are different families with their own species, and their shared form arose separately by convergent evolution, not from belonging to one community.

A student who uses 'adapt' in its everyday sense picks this. Adaptations are inherited features produced by natural selection over generations; a plant does not grow spines because it finds itself in a dry place.

mcqs.q: A biome has long, very cold winters, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil. Which biome is this?
options: Taiga, as in northern Canada
Hot desert, as in Arabia
Tundra, as in Arctic Canada
Grassland, as on the prairies
mcqs.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities
mcqs.explain: Very cold temperatures, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permafrost are the climate conditions that characterize tundra, which supports low-growing plants but no trees.
rationales: A student who treats the two cold northern biomes as interchangeable picks this. Taiga has long cold winters, but its short, mild summers give a growing season long enough, and its precipitation is sufficient, for coniferous forest to grow; a growing season of only a few weeks and permafrost are features of tundra.
A student who identifies a desert by low precipitation alone picks this. Precipitation below 250 mm is shared by hot desert and tundra; the very cold temperatures and frozen subsoil identify tundra.
Very cold temperatures, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permafrost are the climate conditions that characterize tundra, which supports low-growing plants but no trees.

A student who assigns any dry, treeless landscape to grassland picks this. Grassland has warmer growing seasons and, in temperate regions, more precipitation than 250 mm; the frozen subsoil and very short growing season are features of tundra.

mcqs.q: The saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea) of the Sonoran Desert has spines instead of leaves, a thick waxy cuticle, a pleated stem that swells after rain, and roots that are shallow but spread widely. Which statement about these adaptations is correct?
options: The spines are a defence against herbivores and play no part in reducing the water that the plant loses.
The waxy cuticle absorbs dew that condenses on the stem at night, and this is the plant's main source of water.
The stomata open during the day so that transpiration can cool the stem in the heat of the afternoon.
Spines in place of leaves reduce the surface area from which water is lost by transpiration.
mcqs.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
mcqs.explain: Spines are modified leaves. Replacing broad leaves with spines leaves the green stem, protected by a thick cuticle, as the photosynthetic surface, and greatly reduces the area from which water can be lost; the spines also shade the stem and deter herbivores.
rationales: A student who remembers only that spines are sharp picks this. Deterring herbivores is a real benefit, but the primary advantage of leaves reduced to spines is the reduction in transpiring surface area.

A student who thinks plants absorb water through their surfaces picks this. The cuticle is waterproof and reduces water loss; the saguaro obtains water through its wide, shallow roots when rain falls.

A student who believes transpiration is for cooling picks this. The saguaro opens its stomata at night, when it is cooler and less water is lost, and stores the carbon dioxide taken in; daytime transpiration would waste the scarce water.

Spines are modified leaves. Replacing broad leaves with spines leaves the green stem, protected by a thick cuticle, as the photosynthetic surface, and greatly reduces the area from which water can be lost; the spines also shade the stem and deter herbivores.

mcqs.q: The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) lives in the Sahara. It has very large ears with many blood vessels close to the surface, it is active at night and it rarely drinks. How do the large ears help the fox to survive in a hot desert?
options: Heat is radiated from blood flowing near the surface of the ears, cooling the fox without any loss of water.
The ears detect prey moving beneath the sand; their size has nothing to do with body temperature.
The ears sweat heavily, and the evaporation of this sweat is the fox's main way of losing heat.
The ears store fat that can be broken down to release water when the fox has nothing to drink.
mcqs.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
mcqs.explain: The ears are a large, thin surface richly supplied with blood, so heat is transferred from the blood to the air by radiation. Cooling in this way costs no water, which is the scarce resource in the desert; the ears also give the fox acute hearing.
rationales: The ears are a large, thin surface richly supplied with blood, so heat is transferred from the blood to the air by radiation. Cooling in this way costs no water, which is the scarce resource in the desert; the ears also give the fox acute hearing.

A student who thinks of ears only as organs of hearing picks this. Hearing is one function, but the large vascular surface is also a heat-radiating organ, which is why desert foxes have far larger ears than Arctic foxes.
A student who generalizes from human sweating picks this. Sweating would waste water; the fennec cools by radiation from its ears, avoids the daytime heat and shelters in a burrow.

A student who transfers the camel's-hump story picks this. The ears are thin and contain blood vessels, not fat; the fennec obtains water from its food and conserves it by producing concentrated urine.

mcqs.q: The kapok tree (Ceiba pentandra) grows to over 60 m in tropical rainforest, where rainfall exceeds 2000 mm a year and soils are shallow and poor in nutrients because most nutrients are held in living biomass. Which is an adaptation of the kapok to these conditions?
options: Rolled leaves lined with hairs that trap humid air and reduce water lost by transpiration.
Buttress roots that spread out above the ground and support the tall trunk in the shallow soil.
A deep taproot that reaches the water table far below the shallow layer of nutrient-poor soil.
Drip tips on the leaves that channel rain into the leaf blade, where the water is absorbed directly.
mcqs.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
mcqs.explain: The soil is too shallow for deep anchorage, so the kapok is held up by buttress roots that flare out from the base of the trunk and spread the load over a wide area, while a shallow root network absorbs nutrients from the surface litter.
rationales: A student who expects every adaptation to conserve water picks this. Rolled, hairy leaves belong to marram grass on a dry dune; in rainforest water is abundant, and the pressures are light, support and nutrients.

The soil is too shallow for deep anchorage, so the kapok is held up by buttress roots that flare out from the base of the trunk and spread the load over a wide area, while a shallow root network absorbs nutrients from the surface litter.

A student who assumes a tall tree needs a deep root picks this. Rainforest trees have shallow, wide root systems because nutrients are at the surface and water is plentiful; support comes from buttress roots.
A student who thinks leaves absorb water picks this. Drip tips shed water from the leaf surface so that it dries quickly; water is taken up by the roots, not through the leaf blade.

mcqs.q: The black-handed spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi) lives in the canopy of Central American rainforest, feeding mainly on ripe fruit. Which statement about its prehensile tail is correct?
options: Each monkey develops a grasping tail by practice in its life and passes the change to its young.
It was selected for because shortage of water in the canopy is the main pressure on rainforest animals.
It is an inherited adaptation to moving and feeding in the canopy, where it acts as a fifth limb.
It shows that spider monkeys are closely related to other animals with grasping tails, such as chameleons.
mcqs.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
mcqs.explain: The tail has a hairless friction pad and can support the whole body, so the monkey can hang from a branch while both hands reach fruit at the branch tips. It is an inherited feature produced by natural selection in a canopy-dwelling lineage.
rationales: A student who uses 'adapt' in its everyday sense and thinks acquired features are inherited picks this. Young monkeys do learn to climb, but the structure of the tail (its musculature and friction pad) is an inherited adaptation shaped by natural selection over generations; practice does not alter what is passed on.

A student who applies the desert framework to the rainforest picks this. Water is abundant in rainforest; the pressures on a canopy animal are moving between branches and reaching food, which the tail addresses.

The tail has a hairless friction pad and can support the whole body, so the monkey can hang from a branch while both hands reach fruit at the branch tips. It is an inherited feature produced by natural selection in a canopy-dwelling lineage.
A student who equates similar features with close relationship picks this. A chameleon is a reptile; grasping tails evolved independently in the two lineages by convergent evolution.

mcqs.q: Off the mouth of a large river such as the Amazon, the coastal seawater is warm and shallow, but it is diluted by fresh water from the river and carries a heavy load of suspended sediment. Reef-building corals are absent from this water. Which statement correctly explains their absence?
options: Salinity is irrelevant because any seawater is salty enough for corals; only the sediment from the river prevents reef formation.
The sediment carried by the river is a benefit, supplying food to the polyps; reefs are absent only because the water is too fresh.
Reefs would form here only if the water were deeper, because the bright light in shallow coastal water damages the polyps.
River water lowers the salinity below the range corals tolerate and its sediment reduces the clarity of the water.
mcqs.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
mcqs.explain: Two of the five conditions for reef formation are not met. Fresh water from the river dilutes the sea below the salinity that reef-building corals tolerate, and the suspended sediment reduces the light reaching the zooxanthellae and can smother the polyps. Warmth and shallowness alone are not enough.
rationales: A student who does not see salinity as a variable picks this. Sediment does prevent reef formation by reducing clarity, but corals also have a narrow range of tolerance for salinity, roughly 32 to 42 parts per thousand, and river water dilutes the sea below that range; both conditions fail here.

A student who reasons that more particles means more food picks this. Low salinity is a genuine reason for the absence, but suspended sediment is not a benefit: it cuts off light from the zooxanthellae and smothers the polyps, so clarity is a second condition that is not met.

A student who pictures corals as deep-sea animals picks this. Shallow water is a requirement, not a problem, because the zooxanthellae in the coral tissue need light; the absence of reefs here is explained by the low salinity and poor clarity of the river-influenced water.

Two of the five conditions for reef formation are not met. Fresh water from the river dilutes the sea below the salinity that reef-building corals tolerate, and the suspended sediment reduces the light reaching the zooxanthellae and can smother the polyps. Warmth and shallowness alone are not enough.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic B4.1 Adaptation to environment

specStatements.text: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
Finding a limit with a transect
Temperature and rainfall set the biome
Named species in hot desert and rainforest

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Coral reef formation is treated only through the five listed factors. No item, concept or misconception requires knowledge of other conditions sometimes cited (nutrient concentration, wave action, substrate), of coral biology beyond the polyp-zooxanthellae relationship needed to explain the factors, or of other marine ecosystems.

Only the six named biomes are used. No item requires students to distinguish biomes outside this list (for example chaparral, savanna as a separate biome, temperate rainforest or cold desert), and climate conditions are tested descriptively rather than as memorized numerical ranges; where numbers appear in a stem they are given.
